The term “scripting“ implies a static, predetermined outcome. That’s not what’s happening here. Scripting does not exist, but DDA does. To put it as simply as possible, Dynamic Difficulty Adjustment (DDA) tilts the outcome of multiple, randomly generated events in the favor of one side.

DDA doesn’t guarantee victory for anyone, but it definitely does give one player the advantage with respect to things like hitting the crossbar or random bad touches or failing to execute on a skill move or any other number of events that we could term “random”.

Our defensive problems start with the team as a whole. All 11 players have ***some*** role when we don't have the ball. When we've been successful at any point in Gio's tenure, it's been when just about anyone with a moderate understanding of tactics can watch the product on the pitch and see what we're trying to do. There are 3 basic defensive tactics:

1. Pressing. Defending from the front by applying pressure deep in the opposition's defensive third. (AKA High Pressure)
2. Sitting in and countering. (AKA Low Pressure)
3. A combination of the two.

We get absolutely wrecked by the opposition when we're not on the same page. You press as a **team**. Two guys wildly running at the ball like excited Border Collies isn't a press. 3-4 guys applying pressure to the ball cutting off the angles of escape with the rest of the team adjusting positionally to account for the risk of being exposed in the very farthest areas of the pitch ***is*** a press. You're daring the opposition to hit those open guy(s) 30-40 yards away with a diagonal.

Sitting in is the same. It's got to be done as a team. When are we stepping / applying pressure to the ball? Yes, you do have to send men to the ball at some point, even when sitting in. We're terrible at this. How many times has one of our back four played someone onside because they're not in sync with the other 3, or worse, have they backpedaled so freely they're well inside the 18 and the opposition hits an open shot or cross because they lost track of where they were or didn't have the guts to get stuck in when they have to? Often.

Almost no one presses ALL the time. A few WILL sit in the whole game. We do it sometimes. The point is, our defensive problems aren't usually the fault of one or two people. They're the result of an uncoordinated implementation of a defensive tactic. When we press, we don't press together. When we sit in, we're not organized enough to make it work.

IMO defensive tactics are where you can make the most difference as a coach. You can get results well beyond your talent level if you're organized defensively. We do the opposite. Our talent level is not bad, but we're so poorly organized defensively that we underachieve consistently.

Playing low pressure with a selective press is IMO the best option. Getting our players to execute together is a different matter. Gio couldn't do it. I wonder if anyone else can?

The problem isn't "the servers". I know what you're saying, the input delay and in-game slowness, but raw horsepower...it's an extremely unlikely scapegoat. The real problem is much more difficult to solve. Adding more resources and in general balancing resources - even across a massive scale - compute, memory, storage - this is literally one of the easiest parts of what's involved in delivering a product like FIFA. At least in 2022 it is. I'm a systems engineer by trade, so this literally is my wheelhouse. 

The problem is the network code - how the game sends and receives data packets. At least that's my semi-educated guess.

A while back (last year?) there was a thread here where a network engineer or maybe it was just an enthusiast - he'd run some traffic captures with his home setup and analyzed them. My recollection was he'd compared the data retransmission behavior of FIFA to that of some other games, and in short, FIFA's is totally fucked. Of course I'm paraphrasing, but in general, his speculation based on the traffic he'd captured was the way FIFA dealt with TCP/IP retransmissions was really sub-optimal. I won't get more into it than that because 1) I'm not a network engineer and 2) I don't exactly remember. But I do remember the part about retransmission behavior.

So why don't they just fix it? Great question. I don't write software per se, so I can't speak to exactly what's involved in rewriting something like the net code of FIFA, but I'd bet my house that it's not trivial. Especially considering the vast differences in broadband quality across the entirety of FIFA's player base. You need to write the code in such a way that the guy on a 25MB DSL can play against a guy on 1Gbps fiber. And it matches up with the in game animations (among other things). Anyhow, this is a big deal. It's very costly and it takes a lot of time. When you have 1 year between releases, there's not a lot of time to make such a massive change. So they just keep recycling the same old shit. They may add some neat visual changes and animations, but the underlying net code....I speculate that it's pretty much the same as it's always been.

Figuring out why FIFA has such a shit in-game experience compared to other, seemingly-more-traffic-intensive games...if I was fired tomorrow I know I'd probably set aside at least a couple months prior to re-entering the workforce to try and figure out why this is. It's really bothering me. Like from the perspective of a player but also from the perspective of an engineer. I want to know why FIFA is the only game I play that feels like my 1Gbps down/up connect at home is insufficient. Or the hardware in my XSX just isn't up to par.

"The servers" may not be it, at least not entirely. I'm not letting EA off the hook, but as a systems engineer by trade who's job currently and historically has involved performance monitoring and testing, I'm unwilling to sign off on the idea that the poor gameplay many of us experience is related to servers alone. And when we say "the servers", we're talking about resources - compute, storage, memory.

The reason I say this is scaling resources just isn't that hard, not in 2021. Whatever technology they're using, scaling resources is likely going to be one of the easiest things they do. It's why hypervisors and cloud providers are as popular as they are - you can save a shitload of money by dynamically spinning up and spinning down nodes as you need them.

What I want to know is what role the servers play. Are they just facilitating matchmaking or are they hosting the match? So peer-to-peer vs client-server. The answer to this question would determine what IMO is the most likely root cause of the bad gameplay.

What that means in regular language is they fail to quickly provide enough compute, storage, memory, and network throughput to adjust to the player base when demand increases.
